'''Bruno Hasbrouck Zimm''' (October 31, 1920 – November 26, 2005) was an American [[chemist]].  He was a [[professor]] of chemistry and [[biochemistry]] at the [[University of California, San Diego]], and a leading [[Polymer chemistry|polymer chemist]] and [[DNA]] researcher.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Doolittle | first1 = Russell F. | title = Bruno H. Zimm (1920-2005) | journal = Protein Science | volume = 15 | pages = 942–944 | year = 2009 | doi = 10.1002/pro.150942 | issue = 4| pmc = 2242470 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Elson | first1 = Elliot L. | last2 = Qian | first2 = Hong | last3 = Schurr | first3 = J. Mickey | title = Bruno H. Zimm (1920–2005) | journal = Biophysical Chemistry | volume = 121 | pages = 155 | year = 2006 | doi = 10.1016/j.bpc.2006.01.001 | issue = 2| doi-access = }}</ref>

==Early life==
Zimm was born an only child in 1920 in Woodstock, New York.<ref name="biographyProteinScience">{{Cite journal| last = Doolittle | first = RF |year = 2006 | title = Bruno H. Zimm (1920–2005) | journal = Protein Science | volume = 15 | issue = 4 | pages = 942–944 | doi=10.1002/pro.150942| pmc = 2242470 }}</ref> His father was the sculptor [[Bruno Zimm (artist)|Bruno Louis Zimm]], and his mother a writer. Zimm graduated from [[Kent School]] in [[Kent, Connecticut|Kent]], [[Connecticut]] in 1938.<ref>"Sill Society Recognizes Four New Inductees in 2010", ''Kent Quarterly'', vol. XXXVI.3, Summer 2010, p. 42.</ref> After obtaining his Ph.D. in physical chemistry under the tutelage of [[Joseph Edward Mayer|Joe Mayer]] at [[Columbia University]] in 1944, he moved across town for postdoctoral work with [[Herman Mark]] at the [[Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn]], where he began his research on light scattering.<ref name="biographyProteinScience" />

== Career ==
In 1946 he took a position at UC Berkeley, where he continued the work on light scattering and invented the famous Zimm plot for determining both size (molecular weight) and shape factors for large molecules. He then spent most of the 1950's at the General Electric Research Laboratory in Schenectady, New York. After a brief stint as a visiting professor at Yale in 1960, he moved to the University of California, San Diego (UCSD), where he remained for the rest of his life.<ref name="biographyProteinScience" />

== Research ==
In 1956, Zimm extended the [[Rouse model]] of [[polymer dynamics|Polymer Physics]] to include hydrodynamic interactions mediated by the solvent between different parts of the chain.<ref>
Bruno H. Zimm, ''Dynamics of Polymer Molecules in Dilute Solution: Viscoelasticity, Flow Birefringence and Dielectric Loss'', J. Chem. Phys. 24, 269 (1956).</ref> Whilst the original Rouse model overestimates the decrease of the diffusion coefficient D with the number of polymer beads N as 1/N, the Zimm model predicts D~1/Nν which is consistent with the experimental data for dilute polymer solutions, and where ν is the Flory exponent, a measure of the polymer solubility.

In 1959, together with J.K. Bragg, Zimm wrote a classic paper on the helix-coil transition for polypeptides;<ref>{{Cite journal| last = Zimm | first = BH |author2=Bragg JK  | year = 1959 | title = Theory of the Phase Transition between Helix and Random Coil in Polypeptide Chains | journal = Journal of Chemical Physics | volume = 31 | issue = 2 | pages = 526–531 | doi = 10.1063/1.1730390 | authorlink = Bruno H. Zimm |bibcode = 1959JChPh..31..526Z }}</ref>  a year later he published a second paper on the “melting” of the helical forms of DNA.<ref>{{Cite journal| last = Zimm | first = BH |year = 1960 | title = Theory of "Melting" of the helical form in double chains of the DNA type | journal = Journal of Chemical Physics | volume = 33 | issue = 5 | pages = 1349–1356 |authorlink = Bruno H. Zimm | bibcode = 1960JChPh..33.1349Z | doi = 10.1063/1.1731411 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
